Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later

How to sequence bets by the outcome you believe in and the confidence you have earned, instead of by a calendar you have not.

1. A slide Meera Iyer could no longer defend

On the second Monday of March 2026, Meera Iyer, VP of Product at Nadika Systems, opened the deck she was due to present to the board in eighteen days and felt the familiar tightening in her chest. Nadika sold warehouse and inventory-management software to mid-market manufacturers, two hundred and ten employees strong, with customers scattered from Coimbatore to the Gulf. Slide fourteen was the roadmap: thirty-four rows, each tagged with a quarter — Q2 FY26, Q3 FY26, Q4 FY26 — running out to eighteen months. It looked authoritative. It was also, she now suspected, a slow-motion liability.

Two things had collided that week. First, the account team had just closed a ₹1.4 crore renewal with a Ludhiana-based auto-parts manufacturer, contingent on a native SAP Business One connector the roadmap dated for Q3. Second, engineering had discovered, three sprints into that exact connector, that SAP's partner API for the relevant module was more restrictive than the vendor's documentation implied — the honest new estimate was five months, not two. A ₹40 lakh expansion deal with a second customer was riding on the same line. If Meera moved the date, sales would call it a broken promise. If she held the date, engineering would ship something half-working to hit it, and both customers would eventually notice. Either way, the next board conversation would be about a date, not about the business problem the connector was meant to solve.

Meera had inherited the dated-roadmap format from her predecessor, and every quarter it produced the same ritual: stakeholders treated any date as a promise the instant it appeared on a slide, and any slip as evidence that product could not be trusted to plan. She did not yet have the language to describe what she wanted instead, only the conviction that a format built around calendar commitments was structurally unable to tell the truth about a genuinely uncertain SAP integration. What she needed was a way to say, credibly, in the same board meeting: here is what we are certain enough about to commit resources to right now, here is what we believe but have not yet proven, and here is what we are aware of but are not yet acting on — without any of those three statements collapsing back into a date.

2. The idea: sequencing by confidence, not by the calendar

A Now/Next/Later roadmap sequences bets — proposed pieces of work, each aimed at a specific business outcome — into three horizons defined by how much validated confidence the team has in them, not by which month they are scheduled to ship. Now holds outcomes the team has committed real capacity to, based on evidence strong enough to act on. Next holds outcomes the team believes in and intends to pursue, but has not yet resourced, because a specific piece of evidence is still missing. Later holds outcomes worth tracking as part of the strategy, with no near-term plan to generate that evidence at all. The format was popularised in 2017 by C. Todd Lombardo, Bruce McCarthy, Evan Ryan and Michael Connors in their book Product Roadmaps Relaunched, drawing on planning boards already in informal use at companies such as Intercom, whose product team had grown tired of roadmaps that made promises product management had no authority to keep.

The problem it was built to solve is specific: a dated feature list forces a team to state false certainty about things eighteen months out that no one has any real basis to be certain about, and then it punishes the team — through lost trust — for the entirely appropriate act of updating a plan when new evidence arrives. A roadmap sequenced by outcome and confidence instead treats a change in position as information, not failure. This is also why the topic sits downstream of two upstream ideas in a mature planning practice: Rumelt's kernel, which is what makes a roadmap a sequence of coherent actions rather than an unrelated list, and outcome-based prioritisation using strategic themes, which is what supplies the rows the Now/Next/Later board arranges in the first place. The single sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without flinching is this: we sequence by the confidence we have earned in an outcome, not by the calendar, so this roadmap tells you what we believe and how sure we are — not a promise we have not yet earned the right to make.

3. The mechanics, walked through at Nadika

The method has six steps, and the third and fifth are the ones most teams quietly skip. First, start from an outcome, not a feature: Nadika's relevant theme, already agreed at the quarterly strategy review, was "cut days-to-onboard for new manufacturing customers from twenty-one to under ten." Second, generate candidate bets that could plausibly move that number — Meera's team listed five. Third, score each bet on impact if it works, confidence based on evidence actually in hand today, and the effort required, and write the score down rather than trusting a gut-feel ranking, because gut-feel rankings are where hierarchy and the loudest voice in the room quietly override the evidence. Fourth, place each bet into a horizon using confidence and available capacity together, not effort alone — a cheap bet with no evidence behind it does not belong in Now merely because it is cheap. Fifth, and this is the step nearly every team leaves implicit, write an explicit exit criterion for every bet in Next: the specific piece of evidence that would promote it into Now, or demote it to Later. Sixth, decouple review cadence from horizon — Nadika revisited Now every two weeks alongside the sprint cycle, Next once a month, and Later once a quarter — because reviewing a Later bet every fortnight quietly turns it back into a schedule.

Notice what the board does not contain: a single month or quarter label on any card. A reader who wants to know "when" is being asked, deliberately, to ask a different and better question — "what would have to be true for this to move left" — and the exit-test text under each Next card is the answer already written down, so the conversation about timing becomes a conversation about evidence instead of a negotiation over a date nobody can actually defend.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Meera's team scored all five candidate bets against the onboarding theme using a simple formula: score equals impact (rated 1 to 5, how much the metric would move if the bet worked) multiplied by confidence (a decimal between 0 and 1, how sure the team is today, based on actual evidence such as pilot data, customer interviews, or a technical spike), divided by effort in person-weeks. It is a blunt instrument, not a precision one, but writing the number down is what makes the ranking arguable rather than political.

Table 1 — Pass one: scoring five candidate bets against "cut onboarding from 21 to under 10 days"
BetImpact (1–5)ConfidenceEffort (wks)ScoreHorizon, pass 1
E. Hindi/Tamil onboarding videos20.911.80Now
B. Self-serve data-import wizard30.830.80Now
A. ERP connectors (Tally / SAP B1)50.680.375Next
C. Dedicated onboarding concierge40.560.333Next
D. AI-assisted SKU mapping40.3100.12Later

The arithmetic: for E, 2 × 0.9 = 1.8, divided by 1 week of effort, gives a score of 1.80 — cheap, well understood, and nearly certain, so it goes straight into Now. For A, the connector, 5 × 0.6 = 3.0, divided by 8 weeks, gives 0.375; the impact is the largest of any bet on the table, but at eight weeks of committed engineering time against only moderate confidence, the team placed it in Next with an explicit exit test — a two-customer pilot due by 30 April — rather than committing the full build before that evidence existed. That single choice is what would have let Meera walk into the board meeting three weeks later and say the connector was "in Next, validating," instead of "three months late."

Now run the second pass, because a Now/Next/Later board earns its keep precisely when an input changes and the team can show its reasoning moving, rather than a date quietly slipping. Three weeks in, the SAP pilot surfaced the partner-API restriction described earlier: confidence on bet A fell from 0.6 to 0.35, since only two of the five needed integration points now looked feasible this quarter, and the effort estimate rose from 8 to 12 weeks. New score: 5 × 0.35 = 1.75, divided by 12, equals 0.146 — below bet C, so A moves from Next to Later, still visible, still owned, revisit date attached. Meanwhile the churn-risk interviews for bet C had already run ahead of schedule and come back stronger than expected, moving its confidence from 0.5 to 0.65: 4 × 0.65 = 2.6, divided by 6, equals 0.433, now clearing the team's threshold for promotion into Next-with-active-resourcing. Nothing on the slide needed a date changed. What changed was which bets the evidence now supported, and the board updated itself, in public, for exactly that reason.

5. Six distinctions a learner has to earn

"Now" is not "this sprint," and "Next" is not "next quarter"

The single most common misreading is to treat the three columns as a disguised calendar with wider bins. A Now bet can run for two full quarters if the outcome is large; what makes it Now is that capacity is already committed and evidence already exists, not that it will finish soon. The moment anyone on the team privately maps Now to "Q2" and Next to "Q3," the format has been quietly reabsorbed into the very system it was built to replace.

Confidence must be evidenced, not felt

A confidence score of 0.8 has to be traceable to something — a completed pilot, a usage-data pattern, a technical spike that closed off the main unknown — or the whole exercise becomes enthusiasm wearing a decimal point. Teams that relabel a Gantt chart's columns "Now, Next, Later" without changing what evidence is required to move a card have adopted the vocabulary and skipped the discipline.

It sequences bets; it does not choose the outcomes

Now/Next/Later assumes the rows already exist — outcome themes agreed through strategic prioritisation upstream. Applied to an unranked feature backlog with no outcome attached, it simply reorganises the wishlist under new headings. The framework earns its value only after someone has already done the harder job of saying which outcomes matter and why.

Contractual dates need their own lane

A GST e-invoicing compliance deadline, or a bank-mandated audit date, is not a confidence problem — it is a fact with a due date attached by an external authority, and it should sit in a clearly separate lane rather than being forced through confidence-based sequencing, which would either understate the real deadline risk or quietly reintroduce a fake promise into a format meant to avoid exactly that.

It does not tell you if you are overcommitted

Sequencing by outcome answers "in what order," not "how much." A Now column can list four well-evidenced bets that together demand thirty person-weeks against a team with eighteen weeks of real capacity; the board will look disciplined and still be a fiction unless someone separately checks the sum of effort in Now against actual headcount.

It is not a Kanban board, and mixing the two collapses both

Kanban tracks the flow of individual tasks through working states; Now/Next/Later sequences strategic bets by confidence. Placing a Jira ticket for a button colour next to a bet like "expand into the UAE market" on the same three columns erases the level of abstraction that makes the tool legible, and both boards stop being useful for the question each was built to answer.

6. How the same board looks different by business model and stage

At Nirala Foods, a Bengaluru direct-to-consumer snacks brand, outcomes are behavioural and fast-moving — weekly active buyers, repeat-purchase rate within thirty days — and confidence is cheap to earn: an A/B test can settle a Next bet's fate in eight to ten days. Its Now/Next/Later board therefore turns over weekly, and a bet can travel from Later to Now inside a single sprint once a small experiment produces a clear result. At Nadika, by contrast, confidence comes from qualitative signal concentrated in a small number of named accounts — a pilot with the Ludhiana customer is worth more evidentially than a survey of forty smaller ones — so bets sit in each horizon for months, and Now/Next promotion criteria are written around specific customer names rather than statistical significance.

A marketplace changes the picture again. Nazariya Marketplace, connecting home-service professionals with urban households, has to sequence outcomes on both sides of the transaction at once, and a bet on one side is frequently gated by a threshold on the other — a demand-side trust feature cannot be promoted to Now on its own merits if the supply side has not yet reached the liquidity needed to make it meaningful. Practically, this means a marketplace board often needs two lanes, one per side of the market, joined by explicit cross-lane dependency arrows, and a discipline against promoting a bet to Now on early, one-sided data, since network effects take longer to confirm than either a pure consumer or a pure B2B signal.

Stage matters as much as model. A pre-product-market-fit startup usually should not run three horizons at all: when the entire company is still one horizon — find a repeatable reason customers pay — a populated Later column becomes noise that distracts from the single live question, so early teams are often better served collapsing to Now and Next only, with Later reintroduced once the company has more than one live strategic theme to track. A larger company such as Nadika needs Later precisely because it now runs several themes at once; without a visible, actively-reviewed Later, good ideas either vanish silently, which costs trust once people notice, or get dragged into Now anyway, which is how a Now column ends up with twelve rows and nothing shipping.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest way to catch each one

Stakeholders keep demanding a date for a Next item

Symptom: every review meeting, someone asks "so when does the connector ship," and treats "Next" as evasive rather than informative. The underlying error is not stakeholder impatience; it is that no one ever taught the audience what the three words mean before showing them the board. Cheapest diagnostic: ask five stakeholders, cold and separately, what "Next" means on this specific roadmap. If the five answers disagree, the format was never actually introduced — it was only relabelled.

The Now column has twelve rows and nothing ships

Symptom: Now looks impressively full, and the release notes stay thin quarter after quarter. The underlying error is using Now to mean "everything we have agreed matters" rather than "everything we have named capacity for." Cheapest diagnostic: add up the person-weeks the Now column implies and divide by actual engineering weeks available in the period; a ratio above roughly 1.2 means Now is a wish list wearing the wrong label.

A Later bet has not changed in four straight quarters

Symptom: the exact same sentence describing an idea reappears, word for word, at every quarterly review. The underlying error is that Later has become a polite place to file an idea rather than a backlog someone is actively trying to move. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether the bet has a named owner and a specific next validating action; if it has neither, it is not Later, it is a graveyard with the lights left on.

A customer is shown the internal board directly

Symptom: an account manager screen-shares the Now/Next/Later slide to reassure a customer, and the customer later insists they were promised a date. The underlying error is assuming the audience reads column headers the way the product team does; an untrained reader defaults to reading left to right as time regardless of the labels. Cheapest diagnostic: before anything internal goes external, ask whether that specific audience has ever been walked through the format — if not, translate it into plain qualitative language such as "in active development" or "under evaluation" rather than exporting the board itself.

8. What good looks like, six months on

By September 2026, the same theme row at Nadika told a materially different story. Now had shipped: the self-serve import wizard and the localisation videos together had cut onboarding for the SMB tier from twenty-one days to thirteen, measured across forty customers who had onboarded since the change — a real number, not a projection. Next held the concierge pilot, now expanded to ten accounts with its exit criteria tracked on a shared document the customer-success team updated weekly, not a private product artefact. Later still carried the AI-assisted SKU-mapping idea, explicitly dated "revisit after the OCR vendor accuracy study, Q1 FY27," so no one mistook silence for abandonment. In the board meeting, Meera did not defend a slipped date; she walked investors through evidence, and when the Ludhiana renewal came up, the account team could tell the customer, truthfully, that the fix they needed was in Next, backed by a working pilot with a comparable manufacturer, and offer a concrete interim workaround rather than a date they might later have to break again.

9. What Meera decided, and two questions to carry forward

Meera rebuilt slide fourteen around three columns and, just as importantly, around a short glossary slide that came before it, so no board member could read Now as "this quarter" by habit. She wrote an explicit promotion test for every Next bet before the meeting, not after someone asked. She pulled the two genuinely date-bound items — a GST e-invoicing compliance change and a bank-mandated audit — into a separate compliance lane, so a real regulatory deadline would never again be forced through the same logic built for uncertain bets. And she committed, in writing, to a visible note whenever a Later bet was formally killed rather than left to fade, because she had watched what silent disappearance did to trust the first time it happened to someone else's idea. The next things worth her attention, and this reader's, are how large a bet has to be before it deserves board-level visibility at all — the question three horizons and bet sizing exists to answer — and how to run this cadence for years without the review meeting itself calcifying back into status theatre, which is what outcome roadmaps in practice is for.

Two questions worth sitting with.

The last roadmap you saw with dates on it — was anyone actually tracking the confidence behind those dates, or was the date itself quietly standing in for a confidence check nobody had run?

On your own team's Later list, which idea has sat untouched the longest — and would anyone notice, or mind, if it were deleted today?

Case Study · Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Padaav Hospitality Cloud: What Goes in the Now Column

A case on sequencing bets by outcome, prepared for classroom discussion. The case does not resolve.

1. Sunday night in Gachibowli

It had rained all afternoon on 11 July 2027, and from the balcony of her flat in Gachibowli, Devika Rau could hear the water still coming off the awnings of the building opposite. On the dining table in front of her were three printouts: a capacity model her engineering counterpart had sent from Bengaluru at 6 p.m., a churn analysis her customer success director had sent from Singapore on Friday, and a one-page board narrative her chief executive had written himself and marked, in the file name, final-v6. The board pre-read was due to the company secretary at nine the next morning. The board itself would meet on 22 July.

Devika had been Senior Director of Product at Padaav Hospitality Cloud for two years and four months. In April, at the company's annual offsite in Lonavala, Harsh Vardhan Sethi had stood in front of four hundred and sixty-eight employees and promised that Padaav was done with what he called the Gantt chart era. From FY28 the roadmap would be a Now, a Next and a Later; each row would name an outcome rather than a feature; nobody outside the product organisation would be given a date. The room had applauded. Within six weeks, Devika had found three versions of a dated feature commitment circulating — one in a sales deck for a chain in Jaipur, one in a renewal memo for a customer in Colombo, and one inside Padaav's own contractual reporting pack for its largest client in Dubai.

2. How Padaav came to be constrained

Padaav was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Harsh Vardhan Sethi, who had spent nine years as a revenue manager in a mid-market hotel group, and Zubin Mistry, an engineer who had built billing systems for a telecom vendor in Pune. Their first product was unglamorous: a channel manager that kept a hotel's room inventory and rates consistent across its own website and the online travel agencies.

Then came March 2020. Indian hotel occupancy collapsed, and Padaav's India revenue fell seventy-one per cent in two quarters. The company cut forty per cent of its headcount. What saved it was a contract signed on 1 July 2021 with Vaqar Hospitality Group LLC, a Dubai-based owner-operator with seventy-four properties across the UAE, Oman and Qatar. Vaqar committed ₹34 crore over five years and paid ₹12 crore of it in advance. In return, Padaav agreed to two things whose consequences nobody in the room fully priced. The first was a product council: Vaqar would nominate forty engineering weeks a year of prioritised work, and shortfalls would attract a service credit of ₹95 lakh per quarter. The second was a separately maintained build of the platform — internally, the Vaqar Edition — carrying multi-currency handling, right-to-left Arabic layouts, and the municipality fee and tourism dirham logic that the Gulf market required.

The engineering note from June 2021 said the fork would be merged back into the core product "within eighteen months." It was attempted twice, in September 2022 and November 2023, and abandoned both times, each time because a quarter that had been planned for convergence was consumed by something closer to revenue. By FY27 the two builds had diverged across ninety-one files in the rate engine alone, and every feature shipped in the core product had to be re-implemented, tested and released a second time. Padaav's own estimate of the cost of that duplication — the figure printed in Exhibit 2 — was twenty-two per cent of engineering capacity.

3. The industry

India's hotel sector in 2027 was unusually good for a mid-market software vendor and unusually hostile to its customers' margins. Distribution had concentrated. A typical Padaav customer sold between fifty-eight and seventy per cent of its room nights through the online travel agencies — MakeMyTrip and Goibibo, Booking.com, Agoda, Cleartrip, EaseMyTrip — at commissions that general managers described in the fifteen to twenty-two per cent range. Every hotelier Devika met began the conversation the same way: how do I get my guests to book direct.

Padaav competed for budget against established Indian vendors — RateGain in distribution and rate intelligence, IDS Next and Hotelogix in property management — and against the in-house teams of the larger chains. Regulation bore on the roadmap from two directions. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the rules made under it obliged Padaav and its customers to manage guest consent, honour data-principal requests and delete on demand; Padaav's legal counsel had set an internal readiness date of 30 November 2027. GST e-invoicing thresholds had also been tightened, and the Gulf contracts carried their own tax and residency requirements. Exhibit 7 sketches where Padaav's people and markets sat.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence that brought Devika to her dining table is set out in Exhibit 1. Three episodes in it matter more than the rest.

The peak. Between 20 December 2026 and 6 January 2027, Indian wedding season and New Year demand pushed Padaav's rate-push volume above nine thousand updates a minute. The queue behind the OTA connectors backed up. Rates and availability drifted out of sync, and sixty-three properties took bookings on rooms they had already sold. Guest compensation across those properties came to roughly ₹2.7 crore, of which Padaav paid ₹64 lakh in contractual credits. Zubin's team ran a six-week hardening programme in February, declared it complete, and the incident count returned to normal.

What the hardening actually fixed. In June 2027, preparing for the FY28 festive season, Reema Nambiar's platform team in Kochi ran a load test at the volume the sales forecast implied for October — about fourteen thousand updates a minute. The OTA push path held. The metasearch and rate-parity path, which had not been part of February's scope because it had not been the proximate cause in December, failed at 9,400. Reema's memo of 24 June concluded that the February programme had repaired the symptom observed and not the mechanism, and that a repeat at festive volume was, in her words, "more likely than not."

The churn story. Padaav lost forty-one properties in FY27, a gross retention of eighty-nine per cent. Wei-Ling Tan's team in Singapore ran exit interviews; twenty-seven of the forty-one named OTA commission and the absence of a strong direct-booking channel as a reason for leaving (Exhibit 3). That finding shaped the FY28 sales narrative and much of final-v6. In May, Priyanka Sridhar in Toronto joined the same forty-one account identifiers to the incident log and the product telemetry. Thirty-one of them had experienced at least one rate-push failure in the sixty days before they gave notice, and nineteen had had an overbooking event (Exhibit 4). Only twelve had used Padaav's existing direct-booking engine at all in their final quarter. Priyanka circulated the analysis to Devika and Zubin on 2 June. It was not in the board pack.

5. The people

Devika Rau — Senior Director, Product; Hyderabad
Owns the H2 FY28 roadmap and the board pre-read. Position: the Now column should hold one outcome, not six. Incentive: she is the internal candidate for a VP Product title that has been open since January. Not saying: she does not believe the 4.1 per cent pricing number will survive contact with resort properties, and she has not told Harsh so in writing.
Harsh Vardhan Sethi — Co-founder and Chief Executive; Hyderabad
Position: FY28 must have a headline the market can repeat, and that headline is AI-led pricing. Incentive: a Series D conversation he expects to open in the second half of FY29, and a board that has asked for default-alive economics by Q4 FY28. Not saying: he has already described the pricing module to two prospective investors as shipping in the financial year.
Zubin Mistry — Co-founder and VP Engineering; Bengaluru
Position: convergence of the fork is the only change that increases capacity rather than consuming it. Incentive: his engineering budget is frozen at current headcount until Q4 FY28, so his only lever is to remove duplicated work. Not saying: two of the three engineers who understand the Vaqar Edition rate engine have interviewed elsewhere this quarter.
Reema Nambiar — Engineering Manager, Platform; Kochi
Position: the metasearch path will fail again in October, and the twenty-two per cent duplication figure is stale — her own count puts it nearer thirty-one per cent. Incentive: she carries the on-call pager for the peak. Not saying: her thirty-one per cent estimate is derived from three months of her own team's time sheets, not from a company-wide measurement.
Priyanka Sridhar — Principal Data Scientist; Toronto
Position: both her analyses are true and they answer different questions; the churn telemetry is the more reliable of the two. Incentive: the pricing model is the work that gets her cited internally; the churn analysis is the work that gets her thanked privately. Not saying: she excluded twenty-three resort properties from the headline backtest because including them dropped the lift below one per cent.
Wei-Ling Tan — Director, Customer Success (Asia-Pacific & Gulf); Singapore
Position: customers say commission, and customers are the evidence. Incentive: her team's retention target for FY28 assumes a direct-booking capability she has already previewed to at least nine accounts. Not saying: the exit interviews were conducted by the account manager who had just lost the account.
Faisal Al Hammadi — Chief Operating Officer, Vaqar Hospitality Group; Dubai
Position: the forty council weeks belong to Vaqar's guests, not to Padaav's refactoring. Incentive: his own group is standardising systems ahead of a 2028 refinancing and wants certainty. Not saying: Vaqar's technology committee has taken a preliminary briefing from an international distribution vendor.

Nandini Shirodkar of Vindhya Growth Capital chairs the board's product committee and has asked, in writing, for "a roadmap expressed as outcomes with the sequencing logic visible."

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 is the document Zubin sent at six o'clock. It is also the exhibit on which Padaav's senior team least agrees.

7. Voices

"Forty-one customers told us why they left. I have the recordings. At some point we have to accept that the customer knows their own mind better than our event log does." Wei-Ling Tan, email to Devika Rau and Harsh Vardhan Sethi, 9 July 2027
"Both things can be true. They left because commission is killing them. They also happened to have a sev-1 three weeks before they signed with someone else. What I can't tell you from this data is which one moved the pen." Priyanka Sridhar, reply on the same thread, 9 July 2027, 22:41 IST
"Every quarter we defer convergence, we pay it again with interest, and the interest is paid in weeks I cannot hire back. If we do this in H2 we are slow for six months and faster forever. If we don't, in two years the fork is the product and the core is the fork." Zubin Mistry, internal chat, 10 July 2027
"Can someone tell me what Now, Next and Later mean in months? My customers keep asking and I keep making something up." Gautam Puri, sales leadership call, 6 July 2027

8. The options as Devika sees them

Option 1 — Fix the floor

Now: reliability on the metasearch and parity path (Bet D) and the DPDP consent layer (Bet E). Next: revenue science. Later: distribution and convergence. The outcome named is that no property loses a guest or a filing deadline to Padaav. The cost is a board meeting in which the headline is that nothing broke, a Vaqar council commitment left unmet at ₹95 lakh a quarter, and a sales organisation told to carry the same story into a second year.

Option 2 — Sell the ceiling

Now: revenue science and distribution (Bets C and B), the two capabilities carrying ₹23.8 crore of tagged pipeline. Next: reliability. Later: everything else, with DPDP handed to a contracted team and convergence deferred a third time. The outcome named is growth. The cost is that Padaav enters the festive peak on the path Reema has already broken in a load test.

Option 3 — Pay down the tax

Now: convergence (Bet A), with the DPDP layer built once, inside the converged core, rather than twice. Next: reliability and distribution. Later: pricing. The outcome named is capacity itself: between 549 and 774 engineer-weeks a year returned to the roadmap from FY29 onward. The cost is six months in which Padaav ships almost nothing a customer can see, a near-certain dispute with Faisal over whose weeks are being spent, and a Series D story that has to be told without a headline feature.

Devika had written these three on the back of the capacity model, and had then written a fourth line underneath and struck it out: are these actually the choices? Nothing in the three options questioned whether the pricing model had to be built rather than licensed; whether the Vaqar Edition might be priced and sold as a distinct Gulf product rather than merged away; whether consent management might be a capability hoteliers would pay for rather than a cost to absorb; or whether the roadmap ought to be sequenced for the India base and the Gulf base separately, since Exhibit 4 shows that not one of the forty-one churned properties was a Vaqar Edition property.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The pre-read is due at nine on Monday 12 July; the board meets on 22 July, and Nandini Shirodkar has asked for the sequencing logic, not the sequence. Headcount is frozen at 468 until Q4 FY28; the company holds ₹48 crore in cash against a monthly burn of ₹1.9 crore, and the board's stated expectation is default-alive economics by the end of the financial year. The DPDP readiness date is 30 November 2027. Lars Brinkmann is away from mid-September to the end of December, and the direct-booking experience has no second owner. Vaqar's forty council weeks are contractual, its notice date is 31 December 2027, and ₹9.4 crore of ARR — a tenth of the company — sits behind that decision. The festive season begins in the second week of October and does not wait.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Write the outcome each of the six bets in Exhibit 2 is meant to produce, in one sentence each, without naming the feature. Which of the six resist being written that way, and what does that tell you?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 describe the same forty-one properties and point in different directions. What question is each one actually answering, and what would you have to observe to reconcile them?
  3. Exhibits 5 and 6 are the two exhibits most likely to reach the board. Identify, for each, the specific footnote that most weakens the conclusion a reader would otherwise draw — and say who inside Padaav benefits from that footnote going unread.
  4. Bet A returns capacity rather than producing an outcome a customer can perceive. Can such a bet legitimately occupy the Now column of an outcome roadmap, and if so, what outcome is it serving? If not, how does a company ever escape a constraint like the Vaqar Edition?
  5. Padaav's Now, Next and Later have been read inside the company as this quarter, next quarter and someday. Is that a communication failure, a design failure of the framework, or evidence that the sales organisation needs something a horizon roadmap cannot give it? What would you change about the artefact itself?
  6. It is Monday morning. Devika has until nine o'clock. What does she put in the Now column, what does she tell Faisal Al Hammadi, what does she tell Gautam Puri's customers — and, on 22 July, what exactly does she say to the board about the one thing she has chosen not to do?

11. Gachibowli, 11.40 p.m.

Her phone showed a message from Priyanka, sent from Toronto at what would have been mid-afternoon there: Ran it again with resorts included. Do you want the number before you send the pack, or after? Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later

Sequencing bets by outcome rather than by date is the easy half of the idea. The hard half is knowing what the sequence costs, what it hides, and the conditions under which it gives the wrong answer with great confidence.

This page assumes you already know the format: three confidence-ordered columns, outcome rows, evidence-based promotion, no quarters on the cards. What follows is the argument underneath it — where it came from, what it is quietly a special case of, what it charges you, and where competent practitioners who have both read the same books still disagree.

Section oneTwo decisions, two clock speeds

On the morning of 14 October 2026, Kavya Raghunathan, Chief Product Officer of Udanti Grid Systems, sat in a conference room in Hinjawadi with two documents in front of her that could not both be true. Udanti, a 380-person firm that built smart prepaid electricity meters and the head-end software that ran them, had won a contract eleven months earlier to supply and operate 1.1 million meters for a state distribution utility over twenty-six months, under the central government's Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme. The commercial structure was unusual and it was the reason Kavya had taken the job: beyond the per-meter price, Udanti earned four percent of the verified reduction in the utility's aggregate technical and commercial losses, measured annually against a baseline of 18.2 percent on roughly ₹9,400 crore of annual billed revenue. Udanti was not selling hardware. It was selling a number going down.

The first document was the product roadmap, rebuilt that summer into three confidence-ordered columns. Now held tamper-alert tuning and a consumer prepaid-recharge experience. Next held a distribution-transformer energy-balance module, with a named exit test. Later held a line that read on-meter edge inference for tamper detection — revisit after field data volume supports model training, FY28. The second document was a purchase order for injection-mould tooling and a twenty-two-week component reservation, ₹6.2 crore, requiring Kavya's counter-signature by 30 November. It froze the Rev-C board design. And Sreenivasan Y., her VP of hardware engineering, had made the implication brutally plain in a two-line email the previous Friday: edge inference needed 512 kilobytes more static RAM and a step up in microcontroller class. If the Rev-C board did not carry that headroom, the Later card was not deferred. It was dead for four years, because that is how long 1.1 million meters stay on a wall.

This is the first crack in the format, and it is not a small one. Now/Next/Later rests on an implicit premise that deferring a bet is cheap — that Later is a holding pattern rather than a purchase. Kavya was looking at an invoice for the privilege of keeping a Later item alive, and the invoice was due six weeks from Tuesday, eighteen months before anyone would write a line of the software it enabled.

Three weeks later and 840 kilometres south, Tara Fernandes faced the mirror image of the same problem. Tara was VP of Product at Upamaa Systems, a Bengaluru company of 140 people, 61 of them engineers, that sold an AI-native resolution agent to large Indian consumer-service operators — telecom, broadband, direct-to-home television. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹96 crore, of which ₹14 crore sat in a single telecom contract due for renewal in March 2027. The Now column of Tara's board held one very large bet, internally called Setu: a proprietary retrieval and deterministic-arithmetic layer that sat between the language model and the operator's billing system of record. Twenty-two of a planned thirty-four engineer-months were already spent. The premise of Setu, written down and evidenced in July, was that general-purpose models could not reliably perform multi-step prorated billing arithmetic — measured at 71.4 percent exact-match against a held-out set of 1,860 real billing disputes.

On 21 October a model release scored 93.8 percent on the identical evaluation with no retrieval layer at all, at a blended cost of roughly ₹0.42 per resolution against Upamaa's ₹1.90 with Setu in the path. Three of the five cards in Tara's Later column became either trivial or irrelevant in the same afternoon. Her Now bet had lost its reason for existing; her Later column had been partially consumed by a supplier she did not control and had not been consulted by. Anirudh Sen, Upamaa's chief executive, asked her a question at the Monday leadership meeting that she found she could not answer cleanly: if the evidence behind a card has a half-life of about eight weeks, what exactly is the third column for?

Kavya's problem is that Later has a price. Tara's problem is that Later has an expiry date she does not set. Both are symptoms of the same underlying fact, which is the argument this page will make and then test: Now/Next/Later is not a general-purpose planning tool. It is a coarse, deliberately lossy real-options portfolio, correct precisely when information is the scarce resource and time is abundant — and it inverts the right answer whenever that relationship reverses.

Section twoThe idea, its lineage, and the propositions that divide it

Start with a definition tight enough to argue with. A Now/Next/Later roadmap is an ordered partition of a set of candidate bets into three equivalence classes defined by the state of evidence and the state of commitment, where a bet is a named piece of work with an accountable owner, a target outcome expressed as a measurable change in a business or behavioural metric, a falsifiable hypothesis linking the work to that change, and a cost ceiling. Now is the class of bets to which capacity has been irrevocably assigned this period on the strength of evidence already in hand. Next is the class of bets for which a specific, named piece of missing evidence has been identified, and for which a dated activity to generate that evidence exists. Later is the class of bets judged consistent with the strategy for which no evidence-generating activity is currently funded. The crucial structural point, which most treatments elide, is that the partition is defined over evidence states, not over time; time enters only through the promotion rule, and it enters as a date on a decision, never on a delivery.

The lineage is older and less agile than the folklore suggests. Technology roadmapping as a formal practice was built at Motorola in the late 1970s under Robert Galvin and documented by Willyard and McClees in 1987; it was a device for aligning a technology-development pipeline with a product plan with a market forecast, drawn as three stacked time-indexed layers. Philips and Corning ran variants. The academic consolidation came from the Cambridge Institute for Manufacturing, where Phaal, Farrukh and Probert's T-Plan method (2001) and their 2004 survey in Technological Forecasting and Social Change gave the practice its canonical grammar: a roadmap answers where are we going, why, and what do we have to develop and by when to get there, and it is fundamentally a layered, time-indexed artefact.

Software's divergence from that tradition happened in two moves. The first was corruption: through the 1990s and 2000s the technology roadmap collapsed in most software organisations into a dated feature list, a Gantt chart with marketing typography, which retained the time axis and discarded the market and technology layers that gave it meaning. The second was revolt. Janna Bastow, building ProdPad from around 2011, has described drawing three undated columns on a whiteboard specifically to stop stakeholders reading a timeline into a plan she could not defend. C. Todd Lombardo, Bruce McCarthy, Evan Ryan and Michael Connors codified the outcome-and-theme version in Product Roadmaps Relaunched (2017). Marty Cagan went further in Inspired and Empowered, arguing that output roadmaps are the root cause of most of the waste in product organisations. Basecamp's Shape Up (2019) went furthest, discarding the backlog entirely on the grounds that any queue beyond the current six-week cycle is inventory that will rot before it is consumed.

Running underneath all of this, and rarely cited in product circles, is a literature that gives the format its actual mathematical content. Rita Gunther McGrath and Ian MacMillan's discovery-driven planning (Harvard Business Review, 1995) proposed planning to learn rather than planning to execute, with assumption checklists and milestone-triggered redirection. Dixit and Pindyck's Investment under Uncertainty (1994) formalised the value of deferral under irreversibility. Robert Cooper's Stage-Gate gave the discrete-gate architecture. And Donald Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) supplied the sequencing rule — cost of delay divided by duration — and the queueing arguments that explain why an overloaded Now column destroys throughput. Read in that company, Now/Next/Later is a three-bin, low-resolution approximation of a staged real-options portfolio, and almost every expert-level move discussed below consists of recovering some of the resolution the three bins threw away.

The disagreements are sharper than the literature's polite citations suggest, and it is worth stating each school by the specific proposition it would and would not sign.

The outcome-roadmap school — Lombardo and McCarthy, Bastow, Melissa Perri — will sign: a roadmap is a statement of intent and confidence, and its rows are outcomes, not features. It will not sign: a roadmap should contain no dates. Its members are consistently clearer than their imitators that dates belong on commitments that are genuinely commitments, and that the format's purpose is to stop fake dates crowding out real ones.

The empowered-teams school — Cagan, Teresa Torres — will sign: most roadmap items should never be built, and the job is continuous discovery, not queue management. It will not sign: Now/Next/Later fixes the problem. Its argument, which deserves respect, is that the three-column board is a palatable re-skin that leaves the underlying pathology intact: stakeholders still shop from a list of solutions, and renaming the shelves does not stop the shopping.

The commitment school — enterprise delivery leaders, SAFe practitioners, chief revenue officers, anyone who has signed a master services agreement — will sign: a date is a coordination device, not a prediction, and an organisation of four hundred people with contractual service levels cannot coordinate on confidence adjectives. It will not sign: confidence-sequencing is sufficient. This school is routinely caricatured and is frequently right.

The cycle school — Fried and Heinemeier Hansson — will sign: fixed time, variable scope, and no queue. It will not sign: there should be a Next or a Later column at all. Its position is that a card sitting in Later for three quarters is not an option being held; it is an idea being preserved past its expiry so that nobody has to say no out loud.

The real-options school — McGrath, and anyone who has run a capital-allocation committee — will sign: Later is an option, and options have premiums. It will not sign: Later is free. This is the school Kavya has just involuntarily joined.

The single proposition that cleanly separates all five is this: does publishing an undated statement of intent reduce stakeholder pressure over time, or merely relocate it? Sections nine and ten return to it, and the honest answer is that the field does not know.

Section threeMechanics, including the arithmetic practitioners usually skip

Expert practice differs from competent practice less in the shape of the board than in four pieces of machinery that sit behind it: a capacity ledger that is netted before sequencing, a sequencing rule with a dependency correction, a promotion contract that can fail, and a calibration record. Take them in order, on Kavya's numbers.

Netting capacity before you sequence

Udanti's platform group had fourteen engineers, which on a naive reading gives forty-two engineer-months per quarter. That number is a fiction, and the size of the fiction is measurable. Over the four quarters to September 2026, Udanti's engineers spent an average of 34 percent of their time on work that was not discretionary at all: conformance testing against the Bureau of Indian Standards metering specifications, changes mandated by the utility's IT department, security patching, and the monthly reconciliation runs the regulator's audit required. Real discretionary capacity was 27.7 engineer-months per quarter. Teams that sequence against the gross number do not discover their error until the third week of the quarter, and then attribute it to estimation failure rather than to arithmetic they declined to do.

Sequencing: cost of delay divided by duration, and why it fights the obvious ranking

Kavya's team scored six candidate bets against the AT&C-loss theme. For each bet they estimated M, the value to Udanti per quarter if the bet works, expressed in lakh of rupees of performance-linked fee; p, the probability it works, stated as a number they would be willing to be scored on later; D, calendar duration in months; and C, cost in engineer-months. Cost of delay per month is p × M ÷ 3. The sequencing statistic, following Reinertsen, is that cost of delay divided by duration — commonly written CD3 — because under a capacity constraint the correct order is the one that maximises value delivered per unit of the scarce resource, which is time-on-the-critical-team, not money.

Bet E, on-meter edge inference, has the highest expected value of anything on the table — ₹56 lakh per month of delay — and ranks fifth on CD3 because nine months of duration spreads that value thinly across the scarce resource. A board that sorts by "impact" — which is what the great majority of Now/Next/Later boards in practice do, whatever they say — will put E in Now, consume most of a year, and forgo the compounding effect of shipping C and A in the first ten weeks. This is not an argument that E is a bad bet. It is an argument that expected value answers whether and CD3 answers when, and that conflating the two is the most common quantitative error in roadmapping.

The dependency correction, which is where most teams' arithmetic stops being honest

Bet D looks mediocre on both rankings and is in fact the most urgent item on the board, because the head-end architecture at fifteen-minute read intervals is what makes the data for B and E exist at all. The correction is to attribute to an enabler the delay cost it imposes on everything it blocks. D blocks E entirely and caps B's achievable value at roughly 40 percent. Its corrected cost of delay is therefore 54.0 + 56.0 + (0.6 × 47.7) = ₹138.6 lakh per month, and its corrected CD3 is 138.6 ÷ 6 = 23.1 — first by a wide margin. Enablers are systematically under-ranked by every scoring scheme that treats bets as independent, which is every scoring scheme in common use, and this is the mechanism by which platform and infrastructure work gets starved in outcome-oriented organisations that believe themselves to be rigorous.

Capacity now binds. If Now takes D (30 engineer-months) alone, it exceeds the quarter's 27.7 discretionary months, so D is a two-quarter Now bet and nothing else fits — a conclusion the board will resist and which is nonetheless correct. Kavya's compromise was to split D into a 14-month first tranche sufficient to unblock B, run C (4) and A (6) alongside it for 24 engineer-months total, and hold the remaining 3.7 months as slack. Slack is the fourth thing experts do and novices never do.

The promotion contract, and why it must be able to fail

Most Next cards carry an exit criterion of the form "run a pilot with two customers" or "complete discovery with the segment." These cannot fail. A pilot always produces a result, and a motivated team will read any result as encouraging. The expert form states a falsifier and a threshold: if the distribution-transformer energy balance across three test circles does not close to within four percent over sixty days, this bet is killed, not deferred. Kavya's board carried exactly that wording on bet B. The test is easy to apply from outside: ask what specific observation would cause the card to move right rather than left, and if the answer is "we'd have to think about it," there is no promotion contract, only an aspiration with a date attached.

Calibration: the record that makes confidence a number rather than a mood

Confidence scores are worthless unless somebody eventually scores the scorer. Udanti had been logging stated probabilities and outcomes for six quarters. Of twenty-four bets stated at p = 0.8, seventeen delivered the claimed outcome — a hit rate of 70.8 percent, so the team was overconfident by about nine percentage points. The Brier score, the mean squared difference between stated probability and realised outcome, was (17 × 0.04 + 7 × 0.64) ÷ 24 = 0.215, against 0.207 for a team that had simply said 0.708 every time, and 0.25 for a coin. Read plainly: Udanti's judgement carried real information relative to chance, and almost none relative to knowing its own base rate. That is an uncomfortable but usable finding, and the response — shading stated confidences down by roughly ten points and re-measuring in two quarters — is cheap. Tetlock's forecasting work suggests calibration of this kind is trainable; the product literature has almost entirely failed to adopt it, which is one reason confidence columns drift towards decoration.

Second-order effects

Three consequences follow from running the machine properly and are rarely anticipated. First, stakeholder lobbying does not disappear; it relocates to the promotion gate. Where a sales director once argued about a Q3 date, he now argues that the pilot's exit criteria are too strict. This is a substantial improvement — the argument is now about evidence — but leaders who expected peace are disappointed. Second, spikes and research become first-class funded work with named owners, which raises the visible cost of discovery and triggers a predictable finance conversation about why engineers are "not building." Third, and most usefully, the format makes overload visible only if the capacity ledger is maintained; without it, the board makes overload less visible than a Gantt chart did, because an undated Now column has no arithmetic to violate.

Section fourFive conditions, stated as tests, applied to both protagonists

The expert reading is diagnostic: which condition fails determines which part of the machine needs replacing. A C1 failure requires an option-pricing lane, which is Kavya's answer. The first is when the binding constraint is coordination rather than choice: an organisation of two thousand people shipping one integrated release needs a shared time axis more than it needs a shared confidence axis, and confidence adjectives do not synchronise three hundred teams. The second is the half-bridge problem. Now/Next/Later's incrementalism rewards bets whose value is realisable within a horizon, which quietly penalises any outcome that only pays at the end of a multi-quarter arc — a replatforming, a new regulatory licence, a category entry. Teams governed strictly by the format tend to build three halves of three bridges. The third, which section eight documents in detail, is when time itself is the scarce resource: a seasonal window, a launch, a tender deadline. Then the correct plan is a backwards-scheduled calendar, and sequencing by confidence will reliably defer the one thing that had to happen first.

Section fiveHard edges: hardware, platforms, two-sided markets, regulation, AI, and the seams between teams

Hardware plus software: Later has an invoice, and here it is

Return to Kavya's Rev-C decision, because it is the cleanest available demonstration that a Later card is an option with a premium. The full-headroom variant — 512 KB additional SRAM, a higher microcontroller class, marginally larger flash — cost ₹47 of incremental bill of materials per meter. Across 1.1 million meters that is ₹5.17 crore, plus ₹65 lakh of BIS re-certification and conformance retesting, and eleven weeks of schedule risk on the first delivery tranche. Call the premium ₹5.82 crore, payable in full on 30 November 2026.

The payoff, if edge inference works, comes through the performance-linked fee. Udanti's analysis attributed 1.4 of the targeted 6.2 percentage points of AT&C loss reduction to on-meter tamper detection. On ₹9,400 crore of billed revenue, 1.4 percent is ₹131.6 crore of recovered revenue annually; Udanti's four percent share is ₹5.26 crore a year, over the four remaining contract years, discounted at 13 percent — a present value of roughly ₹15.6 crore. At p = 0.40, the expected payoff is ₹6.24 crore against a ₹5.82 crore premium. A ratio of 1.07. Within the error bars of every input, that is a coin flip, and a leader who presents it as a clear yes is not being honest about the estimate of p.

The move Kavya's team found is the one that experts find in this situation, and it is not "decide harder." It is to buy a smaller option. Commercial loss at the utility was heavily concentrated: three of the eleven circles carried 62 percent of it. A two-SKU strategy — headroom on 440,000 meters destined for those circles, standard board for the remaining 660,000 — costs 440,000 × ₹47 = ₹2.07 crore, plus the same ₹65 lakh of re-certification, for a ₹2.72 crore premium. The capturable payoff falls to 0.62 × ₹15.6 crore = ₹9.67 crore; at p = 0.40 that is ₹3.87 crore expected. Subtract the present value of running two firmware trains and two inventory SKUs, about ₹22 lakh a year or ₹0.66 crore discounted, and the direct expected value is roughly ₹0.49 crore positive. Still thin.

The decisive argument is not in the direct arithmetic at all. If edge inference works on 440,000 meters, the Rev-D decision for a 2.4-million-meter tender expected in FY29 is made with data instead of with p = 0.40. The option's dominant value is informational, and it is an option on a future option. This is exactly what Dixit and Pindyck formalised and exactly what a three-column board, which records no premiums and no expiries, is structurally incapable of showing.

Regulated products: commitments are capacity, not roadmap

The standard advice — put compliance work in its own lane — is right and insufficient. A lane still implies competition for attention with discretionary bets, and it invites the annual argument about whether the compliance item is "worth it," which is not a question anyone gets to ask. The stronger practice is to treat externally mandated work as a deduction from capacity before any sequencing happens, exactly as Udanti's 34 percent deduction in section three, and to maintain a separate commitment register — a dated list of everything the firm owes a third party, with the penalty attached — that is reviewed by the same people but as a different kind of object. The register is a liability schedule. The roadmap is a portfolio. Merging them produces a document that is bad at both jobs: it understates the deadline risk, because a regulatory date sits next to cards that can slip, and it corrupts the portfolio, because an item with a penalty attached always wins a priority argument whatever its expected value.

Two-sided markets: confidence on one side is not confidence in the bet

Ubhaya Bazaar, a Jaipur marketplace connecting handicraft clusters to urban and export buyers, ran ₹86 crore of gross merchandise value in FY26 across 11,400 artisan sellers and about 340,000 buyers. In the March 2026 quarter it promoted a buyer-side bet — curated seasonal collections — into Now on evidence that was strong and correctly gathered: a 340-buyer test showed a 22 percent conversion lift. What the test could not see was that matched supply fill rate in the tested categories stood at 47 percent. On launch, conversion did rise, by 19 percent; cancellations rose from 6 to 17 percent, Net Promoter Score fell fourteen points, and the net effect on quarterly GMV was minus ₹40 lakh. The lesson generalises: in a two-sided system the outcome is a function of both sides, so the confidence attached to a one-sided experiment is confidence in a conditional, not in the bet. Ubhaya's fix was a promotion precondition rather than a change in scoring — no demand-side card promotes to Now unless the matched supply cohort holds at least 70 percent fill rate with fourteen days of stable inventory. Rerun two quarters later at 78 percent fill rate, the same bet produced a 24 percent conversion lift, 7 percent cancellations, and about ₹1.9 crore of annualised GMV.

AI-native products: re-index the horizons, do not abandon them

Tara's crisis at Upamaa looks like an argument for shorter planning. It is not. Shortening the horizon does not help when the thing that changed was not the market's preferences but the capability frontier of a supplier. The move that survives a model release is to change the variable the columns index. Confidence-in-outcome is the wrong axis for an AI-native product because it conflates two very different uncertainties: will customers want this, which the team can investigate, and will the underlying capability exist, which it cannot. Separating them yields a board whose columns mean: Now — ships on capability that is generally available today; Next — requires a capability visible in preview, in a published benchmark, or in a provider's stated roadmap; Later — requires a capability nobody has demonstrated. That partition does not get rewritten by a release. It gets traversed by one, which is a very different experience: cards move left on their own, which is a pleasant problem, and the team's job becomes noticing quickly rather than re-planning from scratch.

There is a second, less obvious axis that AI products need and others do not. Upamaa's blended inference cost per resolution fell from ₹3.10 in January 2026 to ₹1.90 by September — 39 percent in eight months. On that trend a bet that is 2.4 times underwater on unit economics today becomes viable in roughly fourteen months with no engineering work whatsoever. The correct encoding is a price trigger written onto the Later card: re-test when blended cost per resolution falls below ₹0.30. This is a genuine departure from the classical format, where cards move because the team learns something. Here the card moves because the world got cheaper, and a board with no mechanism for that will keep rediscovering the same three ideas by accident.

Multi-product and the organisational seams: what mature companies actually do

Udaigiri Financial Cloud, a Mumbai company of about 1,400 people selling nine product lines to banks and non-banking financial companies, provides the multi-product case. Each product line ran a competent Now/Next/Later board. The executive committee asked for a rollup, and received one: forty-seven rows in a consolidated Now column, which nobody read twice. The rollup is not merely unwieldy; it is false. Confidence does not aggregate — a portfolio of nine 0.7-confidence bets is not a 0.7-confidence portfolio, and the union of nine Now columns contains no information about the firm's actual commitments because no product line's Now was set with knowledge of the others' capacity claims on shared platform teams.

What Udaigiri's leadership says it does is align at quarterly planning. What it actually does, and what most mature multi-product firms actually do, is maintain a small number — five, in Udaigiri's case — of named cross-cutting bets with a single accountable executive and a real budget, and permit everything else to be locally optimised with no attempt at coordination at all. The remainder of alignment happens through an informal market in favours between directors, negotiated in corridors and settled over a two-year time horizon of reciprocal obligation. Describing this as a failure of process is a mistake commonly made by people who have just read a framework. It is a reasonable equilibrium: the coordination cost of genuinely aligning nine boards would exceed the value of the alignment, and the five named bets are precisely the cases where it does not. The productive question is not how to make the rollup work but how to choose the five — and the answer, unhelpfully but truly, is that it is a judgement about which dependencies are load-bearing, which is what senior product leadership is for.

The seam that does need explicit machinery is the platform-team seam, where one team's Now is another team's blocked Next. The dependency-inverted view — a board arranged by provider rather than by consumer, in which every platform Now card lists the downstream bets it unblocks and their cost of delay — makes the enabler-undervaluation problem from section three visible at the organisational level. Udaigiri adopted it for its shared KYC and ledger services and found that two platform items sitting in Next had an aggregated downstream cost of delay of ₹1.1 crore a quarter, which had been invisible because it was distributed across five product lines, none of which individually felt it enough to escalate.

Section sixNine distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

One: the expert dates the decision, never the delivery. The folk version of this format says "no dates." Experts' boards are full of dates — 15 January, 28 February, 30 November — and every one of them is attached to a review, a falsifier's deadline, or an option's expiry. The tell-tale sign is a Next card reading decision by 28 February rather than ship in Q1. The obvious reading, that dates are the enemy, is wrong: what corrupts a roadmap is a date attached to an event the team cannot control. A date attached to a moment when the team will look at evidence and choose is entirely within its control, and its absence is what allows Next cards to drift for four quarters in a format that was specifically designed to prevent drift.

Two: the health metric is the demotion rate, not the promotion rate. Ask any team how many bets moved from Next to Now last quarter and they will tell you happily. Ask how many moved right and the room goes quiet. A board on which nothing ever moves right is not a board on which everyone has been right; it is a board on which nothing is being genuinely tested. Experts watch for a demotion or kill rate in the range of roughly a fifth to a third of Next cards per quarter and become suspicious below it. The obvious reading — that demotions are failures and a good team has few — inverts the actual logic, which is that a demotion is the format working: an option was priced, tested and correctly allowed to lapse before it consumed a build.

Three: Later is an option with a premium, and the expert can quote it. This page's central claim in miniature. Ask what it costs this quarter to keep a specific Later card alive and the competent practitioner says nothing, because Later is a list. The expert names the premium: an abstraction kept more general than it needs to be, ₹47 of silicon per unit, a vendor contract renewed at ₹18 lakh purely to preserve the ability to act, an engineer kept current in a domain the company is not currently in. The tell is a Later column with a cost column. The obvious reading — that Later is where free ideas wait — is the specific belief that causes hardware companies to discover in November that a four-year decision was made by default.

Four: the width of the Now column is a throughput statement, not an ambition statement. Competent practitioners size Now by what matters. Experts size it by measured throughput and enforce a work-in-progress limit derived from it, which is usually a smaller number than anyone likes and is frequently three. The tell is that the Now column has fewer cards than the team has engineers, and that someone in the room can state the median cycle time of the last six bets from memory. The obvious reading is that a fuller Now column means more ambition; the queueing arithmetic in Figure 2 says it means less output, and Udanti's own measurements — seven cards, 19.4-week median cycle, throughput down from 2.1 to 1.6 bets a quarter — are a fairly typical illustration.

Five: exit criteria are falsifiers, not activities. Discussed in section three, and it remains the single most reliable field diagnostic for whether a team has adopted the discipline or the vocabulary. The tell is that the exit criterion contains a number and a direction of failure. "Pilot with three circles" is an activity; "balance error must close to within four percent over sixty days or the bet is killed" is a falsifier. The obvious reading — that specifying a kill threshold in advance is rigid, and teams should keep judgement in reserve — is precisely backwards: judgement exercised after seeing the data is where motivated reasoning lives, which is why pre-registration exists in every field that has taken its own credibility seriously.

Six: confidence refers to the outcome, not the delivery. When a competent PM writes 0.6, they usually mean they are 60 percent sure the team can build the thing. When an expert writes 0.6, they mean they are 60 percent sure that building the thing will move the stated metric by the stated amount. These are wildly different quantities — engineering feasibility is typically the smaller uncertainty — and the substitution is almost always unconscious. The tell is to ask, cold, "sixty percent of what?" and listen for whether the answer contains a metric. The obvious reading, that the distinction is pedantic, fails on contact with a board where every card scores above 0.7 because the team is, quite correctly, confident it can write the code.

Seven: the external roadmap is a separate product with its own users. Every treatment warns against showing the internal board to customers. Experts go further: they design the customer-facing artefact deliberately — coarser, with a stated refresh cadence, a named owner, an explicit statement of what it does and does not commit, and an escalation path for the customer who needs more. The tell is that the external roadmap has a version number and a changelog. The obvious reading — that the external view is a filtered copy of the internal one — produces the familiar failure in which an account manager at a channel partner such as Umara Trading LLC in Dubai re-promises a Next card to an end customer three layers removed from anyone who understood the column header, and Udanti discovers it at renewal.

Eight: the board is silent on the hardest question, which is who. Sequencing tells you the order; it says nothing about whether the three people who can actually do the second bet are the same three people doing the first. The tell is that an expert's Now cards carry names, and no name appears on more than two. The obvious reading — that staffing is an execution detail downstream of prioritisation — is how a Now column of three well-sequenced bets becomes a serial queue of three bets all waiting on the same staff engineer, at which point the sequencing was decorative and the real roadmap is that engineer's calendar.

Nine: the expert can name the conditions under which they would abandon the format, and does so without ceremony. A launch with a marketing spend committed, a tender with a submission date, a seasonal window, a hardware tooling freeze, a regulatory go-live: in each of these, time is the scarce resource and the correct instrument is a backwards-scheduled plan with float and a critical path. Practitioners who have internalised the idea switch instruments and switch back, sometimes within one quarter, and do not experience this as inconsistency. The tell is a team that runs a confidence board for eight months of the year and a dated countdown for four. The obvious reading — that mixing methods signals confusion — mistakes methodological tidiness for judgement, and the next section shows what that mistake costs.

Section sevenWhere the differences across product types and stages are real, and where they are not

Much of what is written about tailoring this format to business models is padding. The capacity ledger, the falsifier, the demotion discipline and the calibration record are identical in a consumer app and a defence contractor, and teams that claim their sector is special on these points are usually avoiding the arithmetic. Four differences, however, are real and material.

The cost of evidence, and therefore the natural column dwell time. In consumer products evidence is cheap and fast: a well-powered experiment settles a Next card in eight to twelve days, so the board turns over weekly and Next is nearly a staging area. In enterprise B2B, evidence is named-account-shaped and slow, and a single pilot with a large customer carries more evidential weight than a survey of forty small ones — so cards dwell for quarters, and promotion criteria are written around specific customer names rather than statistical thresholds. This has an under-discussed consequence: in concentrated B2B, confidence and customer request are not independent variables. At Udanti the top three utilities are 71 percent of revenue, so a "high confidence" score frequently means "a large customer asked loudly," and the scoring exercise launders a sales priority into an evidence claim. The countermeasure is to record the source of each confidence claim alongside the number.

Whether value is realised incrementally or at a threshold. Platform products are, contrary to the usual assumption, the best fit for this format, because platform value genuinely is confidence-shaped: a capability is worth what its consumers will adopt, and adoption is exactly what a promotion gate can test. Marketplaces are the worst fit, because value appears only above a liquidity threshold, and a confidence-sequenced board will happily ship four sub-threshold improvements. Hardware sits at an extreme of its own, where value is realised at a manufacturing commitment and the roadmap's job is largely to decide what optionality to buy.

Whether the cost side of the ledger is stable. This is close to unique to AI products and is the reason the price trigger exists. In every other category a bet's unit economics change slowly enough to treat as fixed within a horizon. When inference costs fall by a third or more in eight months, a Later card can become viable through no action of the team's, and boards without a cost-trigger mechanism will simply fail to notice.

Stage. Before product-market fit there is one horizon, not three, and a populated Later column is an active harm — it is a list of ways to feel productive while the single live question goes unanswered. From roughly Series A, two columns become useful because there is now a thing to protect and a thing to extend. Three horizons plus a visible kill list earn their keep once the firm runs more than one strategic theme concurrently, which is typically somewhere between 60 and 150 people. And at scale, most public companies run two systems at once: an internal confidence-sequenced board and an external dated commitment layer covering perhaps 20 percent of capacity. It is worth saying plainly that this dual system is not hypocrisy, provided the mapping between the two is explicit and someone owns it. It becomes hypocrisy at the exact moment the external layer starts being populated by items the internal board has already demoted.

Section eightThree worked examples, including one clear failure

Urjita Mobility Systems: the dull bet that compounded

Urjita, a Chennai firm selling telematics and battery-health analytics for last-mile electric fleets, had 28,000 vehicles under management across 41 operators and ₹41 crore of ARR entering FY26. Its theme was fleet uptime, baseline 88.4 percent, target 94. The glamorous candidate was a battery-swap prediction model; the dull one was normalising the APIs of seven charging networks whose data arrived in seven incompatible shapes. Expected value favoured the model. CD3, after Deepa Nambiar's team deducted 31 percent of capacity for integration and compliance work, favoured normalisation by a factor of roughly two, largely on duration: eleven weeks against thirty-four.

They sequenced dull first. Over three quarters uptime rose to 94.1 percent, logo churn fell from 19 to 11 percent and net revenue retention rose from 104 to 128 percent. The instructive part came later. When the battery-swap model was finally built, it performed materially better than its original specification had projected, because the normalised charging data was by then available as a training input. Urjita could estimate the size of the effect, because a six-fleet pilot region had received the two bets in the opposite order: the model trained on un-normalised data produced roughly 1.8 times fewer correct swap predictions per vehicle-month. Sequencing had not merely deferred the second bet; it had improved it. Cost-of-delay arithmetic does not capture this, which is worth stating as a limitation rather than smuggling in as a bonus.

Ubhaya Bazaar: right method, wrong scope

Covered in section five and summarised in Table 4. The point for this section is that Ubhaya's failure was not a failure of the format but of the unit of analysis: the team scored a bet whose outcome was jointly determined by two populations while gathering evidence about one. The recovery cost one quarter and about ₹40 lakh of net GMV, and the fix was four lines of policy text.

Upavan Fresh: the format gave the wrong answer, confidently

Upavan Fresh, a Hyderabad direct-to-consumer business delivering fruit and vegetables from farmer clusters on subscription, did ₹210 crore of GMV in FY26 across 34 dark stores. Vikram Chitnis adopted Now/Next/Later in January 2026 after a well-run internal workshop, and by every process measure the adoption was exemplary: outcome rows, evidenced confidence, named owners, written falsifiers.

The bet that mattered was cold-chain slot integration with two aggregator partners, plus a customer pre-book flow, aimed at the Banganapalle and Alphonso mango flush that runs roughly from 20 March to 5 June. In February the team scored it at p = 0.45 — they had not validated that customers would pre-book perishable fruit weeks ahead — and placed it in Next with an exemplary falsifier: a 400-household pre-book survey with a threshold of 18 percent stated intent. The survey was commissioned on 2 March and returned on 18 March at 26 percent, comfortably clearing the bar. The evidence was good, arrived on schedule, and was completely useless, because the integration needed six weeks of build and the fruit was already on trees.

The season cost: ₹3.1 crore of foregone mango GMV against plan, ₹68 lakh of spoilage on inventory bought without slot integration in an attempt to salvage the window, and a nine-month wait for the next one. The diagnosis is not that the team was careless. It is that the format's implicit optimisation — spend time to buy information — is correct only when time is cheap relative to information. For a seasonal perishable business, the reverse holds: the window is the scarce resource, information is abundant and merely slow, and any method that trades weeks for certainty will systematically defer the one thing whose lead time made it undeferrable.

The recovery is more interesting than the failure. Upavan did not abandon the board. It built a dated spine of six immovable anchors a year — mango flush, monsoon disruption readiness, Diwali gifting, winter citrus, summer melon, school reopening — each with a lock date computed backwards from the window with float, and hung the confidence-sequenced board off the spine for everything else. Bets that touch an anchor inherit the anchor's date and leave the confidence system entirely; they are scheduled, with a critical path, like the construction projects they resemble. In FY27 Upavan hit five of six anchors on time and mango GMV came in at ₹5.4 crore against ₹2.3 crore the prior year. Vikram's own summary, offered at an industry panel, was blunter than anything in the literature: Now/Next/Later is a method for spending time to buy certainty. If you are in a business where time is the thing you cannot buy, it will lose you a season and look disciplined while doing it.
