Two of these deserve a further word. The invisible-commitment failure is the most expensive on the list and the least discussed, because it is not visible in the roadmap at all — it lives in a bill of materials, an architecture decision record, or a vendor contract. The only reliable detection is a standing question in the quarterly review: what are we currently paying to keep our options open, and which of those options expires before the next review? Most product organisations have never asked it once.

The orphaned-outcome failure is the most common and the most quietly corrosive. It is the natural consequence of a format that makes bets the unit of ownership. A board can be immaculate — named owners, falsifiers, netted capacity, calibrated confidence — and still have nobody whose job it is to care whether onboarding time, or uptime, or loss reduction actually moved. The diagnostic is embarrassingly simple and almost never asked, and the cost of catching it late is that a firm can execute a year of well-sequenced work against a metric that turns out to have been moving for unrelated reasons the entire time.

Section tenWhere competent experts genuinely disagree

Does an undated roadmap reduce stakeholder pressure or merely relocate it? The outcome-roadmap position holds that removing dates removes the false object of negotiation and forces the conversation onto evidence, and points to the observable fact that teams which adopt the format report fewer arguments about slipped dates. The sceptical position — Cagan's, in substance — holds that the pressure is conserved: it moves to the promotion gate, to the definition of exit criteria, and to executive escalation, and the reported reduction in date arguments is a measurement artefact, because the arguments that replaced them were never being counted. The evidence on both sides is testimonial, and it is worth being honest that there is no controlled study of this and probably cannot be one. What would settle it, imperfectly, is a longitudinal count of escalations per quarter across the transition in a large enough sample; nobody has published one. What would have to be true for the optimists to be wrong: stakeholder pressure is a function of unmet demand rather than of artefact format, in which case changing the artefact changes only the vocabulary of the argument.

Should the Later column exist at all? The cycle school's argument is the strongest single critique of the format and is usually dismissed too quickly. Stated at full strength: an item in Later is inventory. Inventory in product development has a carrying cost paid in attention, in architectural generality maintained for nothing, and in the corrosive effect of a list that everyone knows is mostly fiction. Worse, Later lets an organisation avoid saying no, which is the most valuable word a product leader has. Basecamp's practice — no backlog, six-week cycles, every idea re-argued from scratch when its time comes — treats forgetting as a feature, on the grounds that a good idea will resurface and a bad one will not. The counter-argument, from the real-options school and from anyone in a capital-intensive business, is that Later is precisely where option value lives, and that in hardware, platform and regulated businesses, forgetting an idea is not free because the commitments that preserve it must be made years in advance. Kavya's Rev-C decision is a direct counter-example to the no-backlog position. Tara's October is a direct counter-example to the keep-everything position. What would have to be true for the cycle school to be right in general: that the carrying cost of held options exceeds their exercise value across most businesses, which is plainly true for pure software with short lead times and plainly false for anything with tooling.

Is confidence quantifiable at all? One camp says yes: forecasting research demonstrates that calibration is trainable and measurable, Brier scores give a real feedback loop, reference-class forecasting in the Flyvbjerg tradition reliably beats intuition on project outcomes, and Monte Carlo throughput forecasting on historical cycle-time data beats expert estimates on delivery questions. The other camp, drawing on Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein's work on noise, says the numbers are theatre: a 0.6 and a 0.7 are indistinguishable given the noise in the judgement producing them, writing them down confers unearned authority, and the arithmetic performed on them — multiplying by impact, dividing by effort — compounds noise rather than cancelling it. Both camps have a point and they are not fully reconcilable. The partial synthesis that most experienced practitioners actually operate, without quite endorsing it, is that the numbers are worthless as absolute estimates and useful as a forcing device: the act of writing 0.4 rather than "medium" provokes the question why not 0.6, and the argument that follows is where the value is. That is an uncomfortable defence, because it concedes the sceptics' epistemics and keeps the practice anyway.

Should roadmaps be customer-facing? The transparency position, associated with developer-tools and open-source-adjacent companies, holds that a public roadmap is a discovery instrument and a trust-builder, and that the discipline of publishing improves internal honesty. The opposing position holds that a published roadmap is a contract regardless of the disclaimers on it, that enterprise procurement will treat it as one, and that Upamaa's Annexe C is the predictable end state. Both are describing real experience in different market structures: in a high-volume, low-contract-value business, publishing is close to costless; in a business where three customers are 71 percent of revenue, it is a legal exposure. The disagreement is therefore less about roadmaps than about customer concentration, which is a more tractable question than either camp usually admits.

Whose document is it? The quietest disagreement and perhaps the most consequential. One view holds the roadmap is a product-team artefact, owned by the people doing discovery, with executives as an audience. The other holds it is a capital-allocation artefact, owned by the executive who controls the budget, with product teams as the authors. The practical fault line is who may promote a card. Organisations rarely make this explicit, which is why promotion decisions are so often re-litigated: two people both believe, sincerely and for defensible reasons, that the decision was theirs. No framework resolves this, and the pretence that Now/Next/Later is a neutral format obscures the fact that adopting it is itself a move in that argument — it shifts authority towards whoever controls the evidence.

Section elevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this material can build a good board. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They are unembarrassed about switching instruments. Asked for a roadmap, they ask first what decision the artefact is meant to support and for whom, and are equally comfortable producing a confidence board, a backwards-scheduled critical path, or a one-page commitment register, sometimes all three for the same quarter. They do not experience this as inconsistency and do not defend the format as a belief system.

They price things that other people treat as free. Deferral, optionality, generality, slack, the second SKU, the abstraction kept one layer more flexible than today requires. Their planning documents contain costs for decisions not yet taken, which is the single most reliable signature of the difference, and it is the reason Kavya found the two-SKU answer while a competent version of her would have found only a yes-or-no on ₹5.82 crore.

They maintain a memory. A calibration log, a kill list with dates and reasons, a record of what the team believed twelve months ago about the bets it has since shipped. This is tedious, unglamorous and almost entirely absent from product organisations, and it is what converts confidence from a mood into an instrument. Teams with such a record argue differently: the question "are we usually right when we say 0.8?" has an answer, and the answer ends arguments that otherwise run for hours.

They treat the roadmap as a claim about the world that can be wrong, rather than as a plan to be defended. The behavioural tell is how they open a review. A competent practitioner opens by reporting progress. An expert opens by naming what they now believe that they did not believe last time, and what evidence changed it — including, frequently, that a bet they championed should be killed. This is not humility as a virtue; it is the only posture from which the format's machinery does anything at all.

Section twelveWhat Kavya and Tara decided

Kavya signed the tooling purchase order on 27 November 2026 in the two-SKU configuration: RAM headroom on 440,000 meters destined for the three high-loss circles, standard board on the remaining 660,000. The direct expected value was thin, roughly ₹0.49 crore, and she said so to her board rather than dressing it up; the decisive argument she put in writing was that the option's real payoff was informational — a de-risked Rev-D decision for the 2.4-million-meter tender expected in FY29. She then made two changes to the roadmap itself. She added a premium column to Later, so that every card in it carries what it costs this quarter and when it expires, with zero written explicitly where the premium is genuinely zero. And she moved the AT&C-loss commitment schedule out of the roadmap entirely into a commitment register with the liquidated-damages clause attached to each milestone, on the reasoning that a liability schedule and a portfolio are different objects and a document that tries to be both is reliably bad at each.

Tara took eleven days and then killed Setu, writing off fourteen of twenty-two engineer-months and salvaging eight — the parts concerned with authenticated write access to the operator's system of record, which no model release makes unnecessary. She re-indexed the three columns on capability dependence rather than confidence, added price triggers to two Later cards, and instituted a six-week model-release review with an explicit mandate to rewrite the board, so that the next release would arrive as an input to a scheduled process rather than as a crisis. The Annexe C problem she could not fix unilaterally; she opened a conversation with the operator's procurement team to replace the enumerated roadmap with a service-level commitment on resolution rate and cost per contact — which is what the customer actually wanted, and which Upamaa could now meet more cheaply than when the annexe was written. Anirudh's strategy question she escalated rather than answered, on the grounds that section four's fifth condition had failed and no amount of board hygiene would compensate.

Discussion questions

1. Kavya's two-SKU option carried a direct expected value of about ₹0.49 crore on inputs — particularly p = 0.40 — that are themselves guesses. At what value of p does the decision reverse, and does the informational argument about the FY29 tender survive that reversal, or is it a rationalisation constructed to justify a decision already made on instinct?

2. Upavan Fresh ran the format correctly and lost a season. Was the error in the method, in Vikram's application of it, or in the prior question of which method the business needed — and how would a product leader arriving at Upavan in January 2026 have known, before the mango flush, which of those three it was?

3. Tara's re-indexing makes Upamaa's board robust to model releases by moving the uncertainty she cannot control onto the column definitions themselves. What does this cost her? Specifically: what can her board no longer express that a confidence-indexed board could, and which of her stakeholders will notice first?

Section thirteenGoing deeper

Rumelt's kernel. Section four's fifth condition is the one whose failure invalidates everything else; the kernel — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — is the test for whether the rows on your board are a strategy or a wish list. Unlocks the ability to tell the difference before you spend a quarter sorting noise.

Strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation. The upstream process that produces the rows Now/Next/Later arranges. Worth studying next because almost every diagnosed roadmap failure turns out, on inspection, to be a prioritisation failure wearing a sequencing costume.

The roadmap as communication. Nuance seven argued the external roadmap is a separate product with its own users; this topic is where that product gets designed, versioned and owned.

Annual and quarterly planning. The cadence into which the board's promotion decisions must land, and the arena where the capacity ledger either becomes real or becomes an exercise. Unlocks the negotiation between a confidence-sequenced portfolio and an annual budget.

Milestones and release planning. The instrument you switch to when time is the binding constraint — Upavan's dated spine, Kavya's tooling freeze. Mastery is knowing which of the two you are holding.

Three horizons and bet sizing. Frequently confused with Now/Next/Later and measuring something entirely different: business maturity rather than evidence state. Worth studying precisely to stop the conflation, and to learn how large a bet must be before it needs board-level visibility.

Outcome roadmaps in practice. The operational detail of running this for years without the review meeting calcifying into status theatre — cadence design, artefact hygiene, and the demotion rituals that keep the format honest.

Strategy vs roadmap vs plan. Three artefacts routinely merged into one document that serves none of them; Kavya's decision to split the commitment register out of the roadmap is this distinction applied.

OKRs and goal setting. The mechanism that attaches an owner to the outcome rather than to the bets, which is the orphaned-outcome failure mode in Table 5 and the hardest one to see.

Capacity planning. Section three's netting exercise, done properly: the difference between headcount and discretionary engineer-months, and the queueing consequences of loading a Now column above about 80 percent.

Dependency management. The dependency correction that moved Udanti's bet D from fourth to first, and the dependency-inverted board that made ₹1.1 crore a quarter of distributed delay cost visible at Udaigiri.

When dates matter: launches, seasons, contracts. The explicit treatment of the case this page argues the format handles worst. Read it directly after Upavan Fresh.

Customer-facing roadmaps. The disagreement in section ten about publication, worked through as a practice: what to publish, at what resolution, with what refresh commitment, and how customer concentration changes the answer.

Ekatra Commerce Cloud: The Now / Next / Later Decision

Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — sequencing bets by outcome, not as a dated feature list

1. The scene

On the morning of 12 January 2027, Ananya Deshpande sat in Ekatra Commerce Cloud's fourth-floor office on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road, rewriting the same slide for the fourth time. As Vice President of Product, she had eleven days before the board meeting on 23 January to present the H1 FY28 roadmap — the plan that would tell the company's two engineering pods, its investors, and its largest customers what Ekatra would build next, and in what order. She had three strong, well-argued, mutually exclusive claims on that roadmap, enough engineering capacity for only one of them to start immediately, and a board that had been told, after a rocky Diwali quarter, that this roadmap would be "outcome-led, not a wish list." Ananya's problem was not a shortage of good ideas. It was sequencing them so that the reasoning, and not just the dates, would survive contact with the board.

2. Company background

Ekatra Commerce Cloud was founded in 2017 by two former Flipkart supply-chain engineers to solve a problem they had lived: mid-market Indian retailers and D2C brands selling across five or six channels — their own website, Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, and increasingly quick-commerce apps such as Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart — had no single system to see stock, route orders, and reconcile payouts. Ekatra's order-and-inventory-management (OMS) platform sat in that gap. By January 2027 it served roughly 260 retail and D2C brands, carried ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue, and employed 210 people, engineering split between Bengaluru and Pune. Its closest competitors, Increff and Unicommerce, offered similar plumbing. Ekatra's pitch to the board had always been that discipline in what it built, not the size of its feature list, was what kept it ahead of better-funded rivals.

3. The situation

Three separate pressures had converged on the same planning cycle, each carried to Ananya by a different member of her global team, each certain that their case was the obvious Now.

The first was commercial and urgent. Rohan Mehta, Ekatra's sales head, worked out of Edison, New Jersey. His most pressing account was Tanoor Retail Group DMCC, a Dubai-based hypermarket chain and Ekatra's single largest customer at ₹6 crore in annual contract value, up for renewal on 1 April. Tanoor's operations head had told Rohan bluntly that renewal depended on a custom same-day delivery-routing module built to Tanoor's warehouse layout in Jebel Ali, a request no other customer had made.

The second pressure was strategic and slower-burning. The Open Network for Digital Commerce, the government-backed ONDC network, had grown steadily through 2026, and a rising share of Ekatra's mid-market customers were asking, unprompted, when Ekatra would let them sell through the network without paying Flipkart's or Amazon's commission. Both Increff and Unicommerce had shipped ONDC connectors the previous quarter. Ekatra had none. No single customer was threatening to leave over it, but Meera Vaidya, who ran customer success from Singapore and spoke to renewal-risk accounts daily, warned that the absence was starting to show up as a reason mid-tier customers gave for evaluating competitors during renewal calls.

The third pressure was operational and, in Ananya's private judgment, the most dangerous. Karthik Subramaniam, Ekatra's engineering lead in Pune, and Alex Petrov, a data scientist working out of Toronto who modelled platform load, had spent December reconstructing what happened during the Diwali quick-commerce peak: Ekatra's inventory-sync engine, built for hourly reconciliation, had buckled under the fifteen-minute delivery-slot cadence that quick-commerce channels now demanded, causing stock-count errors that led nine customers to oversell and then cancel orders during the highest-traffic week of the year. Karthik's estimate was that a comparable failure during the next big sale event — Republic Day promotions were six weeks away, the bigger one, the summer end-of-season sale, five months out — could touch the majority of Ekatra's customer base at once, not one account.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A — Tanoor first

Commit the routing module to Now, the sync re-architecture to Next, and the ONDC connector to Later. This protects the ₹6 crore renewal well ahead of the 1 April deadline and keeps Rohan's largest relationship intact. Its cost is that Ekatra enters the Republic Day and summer sale peaks with the same sync engine that failed at Diwali, and pushes the ONDC connector a further two quarters behind Increff and Unicommerce.

Option B — Reliability first

Commit the sync re-architecture to Now, the ONDC connector to Next, and the Tanoor module to Later, offered in the interim as a manual, services-supported workaround rather than a platform feature. This treats the outcome of "no customer loses an order to a sync failure" as the highest-leverage bet, since it protects all 260 accounts through two peak-selling seasons rather than one account's renewal. Its cost is real: Tanoor may not accept a workaround, and losing 15.8% of ARR during the renewal window is a visible wound that a prevented outage is not.

Option C — Network first

Commit the ONDC connector to Now, the sync re-architecture to Next, and the Tanoor module to Later. This answers the market signal directly, closes the competitive gap with Increff and Unicommerce, and gives Meera's team a concrete date to offer nervous mid-tier renewals. It leaves the sync engine unfixed through the nearer Republic Day peak and does nothing, in the short term, for the Tanoor renewal risk.

7. Questions for discussion

  • What outcome, stated in one sentence, is each of the three candidate bets actually meant to produce — and which outcome, if left unaddressed for two quarters, does the most damage to Ekatra as a whole?
  • Exhibit 1 shows that no two bets fit inside one quarter's capacity. What does that imply about sequencing by outcome rather than by stakeholder?
  • How should Ananya weigh a concentrated, certain loss (Tanoor's ₹6 crore, 15.8% of ARR) against a diffuse, probable one (a repeat sync failure touching an unknown number of the other 260 accounts)?
  • If Ananya chooses Option B, what should she tell Rohan Mehta to say to Tanoor before 1 April, and what should she tell the board about why Tanoor is Later and not Now?

8. A note for the learner

The lens this case asks you to apply is simple to state and hard to hold onto under pressure: a roadmap sequences bets by the outcome each one produces, not by the loudest requester or the nearest deadline. The discipline of Now/Next/Later is not choosing whose evidence is strongest; it is asking which outcome, if delayed, compounds against the business as a whole, and which can survive an interim answer.

A well-reasoned answer works through Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 explicitly: it names the outcome behind each bet, tests it against the capacity constraint that forces a real trade-off, and does not let a single large account's ARR silently outweigh a platform-wide reliability risk simply because the account's number is easier to put in a slide.

The defensible path is Option B. The sync-engine failure is the only one of the three risks that scales with Ekatra's entire customer base, and it grows worse, not better, the longer it waits. Reliability is also the input the other two bets quietly depend on: an ONDC connector built on an unreliable sync engine inherits the same failure mode, and a custom routing module for Tanoor is worth little to a customer whose stock counts cannot be trusted during a sale. Choosing Option B does not make the Tanoor risk disappear, and a defensible plan treats that risk on its own terms: Rohan should carry a dated commitment for the routing module in Next, backed by a named services engineer for the interim workaround, so the renewal conversation is about sequencing, not refusal. The board slide that survives contact, in other words, is not the one with the most features by April. It is the one that can say, in a single sentence, why this outcome first keeps the other two possible at all.
